- Model consistently overestimates prices, especially in early forecast periods (first 5–10 days), suggesting a bias toward higher values.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., 71.17, 72.65), model forecasts overshoot and fail to correct downward quickly — exhibit lagged reaction to volatility.
- Mean reversion is underappreciated: model fails to anticipate gradual decline after peaks, often holding high forecasts longer than observed.
- Forecasts for the last 5–10 days of the 30-day window are often too high, suggesting poor tail behavior modeling or horizon-specific overconfidence.
- Model exhibits strong bias toward higher values in the first half of the forecast window, then gradually adjusts — but often adjusts too late or too much.
- When history shows a clear downward trend (e.g., 72.52 → 65.56), model fails to reflect the full extent of the decline, underestimating the drop.
- Model tends to overreact to recent high values, creating artificial “peaks” in forecast that don’t align with true price behavior.
- Forecasts often fail to capture the “slow decay” phase after a spike — model assumes faster reversion than observed.
- Model underestimates the magnitude of corrections after a spike, especially in the 10–20 day window post-peak.
- Model shows persistent bias toward overestimating the 30-day average, especially when recent history is volatile.
